high.title: Dollar-Won Rate to Fall in Q3... Opportunity for Won-Denominated Bonds in Three Months
high.summary:
DB Securities researcher Moon Hong-chul projects in the firm's July outlook report that the KRW/USD exchange rate will face **near-term upward pressure** (i.e., Won weakness) before potentially declining in Q3. The key driver cited is **passive fund rebalancing**: foreign investors' share in the domestic equity market has grown excessively, and portfolio rebalancing flows are expected to temporarily weigh on the Won as foreign capital rotates out of Korean equities. However, with oil prices stabilizing and interest rates taking a breather, the analyst sees the exchange rate headwinds as temporary. The core investment thesis is that **won-denominated bonds present a buying opportunity in approximately three months**, once the FX and rate volatility subsides. For FX traders, this signals near-term KRW softness before a potential Q3 reversal — a classic "wait and reload" setup. Bond investors should monitor the pace of foreign equity outflows and stabilization in global rates as the key triggers. This is directly actionable for KRW and KTB positioning.

---

high.title: [FX-Weekly] Dollar-Won Tests 1,550 Level Amid US-Iran Military Clash - Authorities' Intervention in Focus
high.summary: The USD/KRW exchange rate is expected to trade around the 1,540 won level this week (June 29–July 3), with upside risk toward the 1,550 level driven by two converging pressures: geopolitical uncertainty stemming from the US-Iran military confrontation and sustained foreign equity selling on the domestic Korean stock market. Last week, the pair gradually drifted higher, trading within a 1,530–1,540 range as foreign investors maintained a clear selling posture in Korean equities, generating USD demand and KRW supply pressure.

high.title: Dollar-Won Takes Breather in Overnight Trading, Closes at 1,543.00 Won
high.summary: The USD/KRW exchange rate closed at 1,543.00 won at 2:00 AM KST on June 30, representing an 11.00 won gain from the prior Seoul FX market close. Notably, the pair had surged more than 13 won during Seoul's regular session, driven predominantly by heavy foreign selling of Korean equities — a clear signal of risk-off capital outflows from the Korean market. The won subsequently recovered a portion of those losses during New York trading hours as the broader US dollar softened.

high.title: Key Finance Ministry Officials Leave for Private Sector - Former Bond, FX Authorities Also Depart
high.summary: The departure of director-level officials from Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance — specifically those who oversaw **government bond and foreign exchange market policies** — represents a meaningful institutional development for KRW and KTB market watchers. These are core working-level technocrats who shaped day-to-day market policy, intervention frameworks, and bond issuance strategies. Their exit into the private sector is part of a broader talent exodus across Korea's public sector.

medium.title: Deputy PM Koo Yun-chul: Full Government Support for Corporate Regional Investment, Signals Industrial Policy Focus
medium.summary:
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Koo Yun-chul publicly committed to full government support for companies investing in South Korea's regional provinces, framing it as critical to maintaining global competitiveness in advanced industries. While primarily a domestic industrial policy statement, commentary from the Finance Minister carries macro relevance — particularly in signaling a pro-growth, pro-investment fiscal stance that could influence government spending and bond issuance. Any fiscal expansion to support regional investment incentives could have marginal implications for Korean government bond supply dynamics. International fund managers should watch for follow-up fiscal policy announcements, as increased government spending could affect KTB yield curves and KRW sentiment through fiscal balance channels.

---

medium.title: [New York FX Market - Weekly] Japan Intervention Fears Persist as US Jobs Data Complicates Market Calculus
medium.summary: The dollar is expected to open the week on a firm footing globally, driven by weekend US-Iran military developments. Dollar-Yen is approaching the 162 level, a zone widely considered a potential trigger for Japanese FX intervention. Weaker-than-expected US jobs data could complicate the dollar's trajectory — if payrolls disappoint, it would reinforce Fed rate cut expectations, potentially capping broad dollar strength and offering some relief to KRW. The ECB Sintra Forum is also in focus, with potential global monetary policy coordination signals that could shift cross-currency dynamics. For KRW traders, this article is relevant as a broader USD directional guide — a stronger dollar environment globally tends to reinforce USD/KRW upside, while any dollar pullback on soft US data would provide KRW relief. Watch Friday's US NFP print as the week's key macro catalyst.

medium.title: Iran Warns Against Attempts to Bypass Hormuz Strait Route - 'Will Escalate Tensions'
medium.summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed at a Baghdad press conference that management of Strait of Hormuz maritime traffic remains Iran's responsibility following a US-Iran agreement, while warning that attempts to bypass the route will escalate tensions. This is directly relevant to Korean financial markets given Korea's extreme dependence on Middle East energy imports — approximately 70%+ of Korea's crude oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz. Any sustained disruption or escalation would materially widen Korea's trade deficit, pressure the current account, and add structural KRW depreciation risk. Elevated oil prices flowing from Hormuz tensions would also feed into Korean inflation dynamics, potentially complicating BOK's monetary easing path. Bond investors should watch whether oil-driven inflation expectations begin repricing the short end of the Korean yield curve.

medium.title: Margin Debt Hits 38 Trillion Won - FSS Chief Lee Chan-jin Vows Enhanced Monitoring
medium.summary: Korea's Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) Governor Lee Chan-jin has announced enhanced monitoring of leveraged stock purchases ("bittoo" — debt-fueled investing) as margin debt has surged to 38 trillion won, with individual credit loans rising 18 trillion won above historical averages last month. While primarily a financial stability concern, this development carries indirect macro relevance: elevated leverage in equities increases systemic vulnerability to sharp market corrections. A rapid unwind of leveraged positions could trigger forced equity selling, amplifying foreign outflow dynamics and adding pressure to KRW. The FSS's heightened oversight posture may also signal broader macroprudential tightening, which could have implications for domestic credit conditions and indirectly influence BOK's policy flexibility. Watch for any formal regulatory measures announced in coming weeks.

medium.title: US Supreme Court Temporarily Blocks Trump's Dismissal of Fed Governor Lisa Cook (Comprehensive)
medium.summary: The US Supreme Court ruled 5-4 to block President Trump's attempt to dismiss Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, upholding a lower court injunction while litigation over the legality of her dismissal continues. The court noted Cook had not received prior notice or opportunity to respond. Governor Cook stated the ruling "recognizes the importance of Fed independence." This development is meaningful for KRW and Korean bond markets as it reduces near-term uncertainty around potential politicization of the Federal Reserve. Perceived preservation of Fed independence is supportive of USD credibility and helps anchor US rate expectations, which in turn limits disorderly moves in EM currencies including KRW. Fund managers should continue to monitor how this legal battle evolves, as any renewed threat to Fed independence could introduce additional volatility into global rate and FX markets.

medium.title: US Treasuries Mixed in Tight Range After Hormuz Clashes
medium.summary: US Treasury markets traded in a cautious, directionless range following military exchanges between the US and Iran in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, with the 10-year Treasury yield standing at 4.379% (up ~0.5 bps) as of 9:17 AM ET on June 29. The mixed price action reflects competing forces: safe-haven demand from geopolitical risk versus inflationary concerns tied to potential oil supply disruptions through the Strait. For Korean markets, elevated US 10-year yields above 4.35–4.40% maintain upward pressure on Korean government bond yields and reinforce the interest rate differential that has weighed on KRW. Geopolitical escalation in the Strait of Hormuz also poses an indirect risk to Korea as a major oil importer, with potential pass-through to inflation and the current account. Watch for further developments in US-Iran tensions as a key macro risk variable.

medium.title: National Pension Fund Nears 1,700 Trillion Won Mark with 60% Return on Domestic Stocks Through April
medium.summary: South Korea's National Pension Service (NPS) grew its total assets to **1,671 trillion won (~$1.27 trillion)** by end-April, driven by a remarkable 59.71% return on domestic equities and an overall fund return of 14.18% year-to-date. The NPS is one of the largest institutional players in both Korean equities and government bonds, and its asset allocation decisions have direct implications for domestic capital flows. Strong domestic equity outperformance may prompt the NPS to rebalance — potentially selling Korean stocks and rotating into overseas assets or bonds — which could weigh on the KOSPI and influence KRW flows. International fund managers should monitor NPS rebalancing signals closely, as large-scale foreign asset purchases by the NPS historically create structural KRW selling pressure.

medium.title: German Asset Manager DWS Says Korean Stocks Still Cheap, MSCI Developed Market Inclusion 'Matter of Time'
medium.summary: DWS Global Head of Research Johannes Mueller expressed a constructive view on Korean equities, noting valuations remain attractive and that MSCI Developed Market index inclusion — again deferred in the latest review — is inevitable in the medium term. MSCI reclassification remains a structural catalyst for **foreign capital inflows** into Korean equities and by extension KRW appreciation. DWS's public endorsement from a major global asset manager may reinforce foreign investor interest in Korean markets. For KRW and bond traders, sustained foreign equity inflows would provide a supportive technical bid for the won, while MSCI inclusion anticipation could attract pre-positioning flows. Watch for any formal timeline signals from MSCI in upcoming reviews.
